name: LABRI (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the one policy whose expected value is counted is the Philippines', so the children and adults protected are in the Philippines.
summary: LABRI (the Lead-Acid Battery Recycling Initiative) works with governments to stop used car and motorbike batteries being melted down in backyards, which spreads lead into the air and soil; in the Philippines it has proposed, with the environmental regulator, making battery makers and importers responsible for licensed recycling, and is now designing that policy with government and industry. We count its spending from April 2025 to October 2026 against that work's expected value: the chance the policy is adopted, times the blood lead Philippine children would lose, valued as later earnings, with adults' heart-disease deaths as a side effect. At the defaults it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000. Nothing has been adopted yet, the charity publishes no accounts and nobody has measured how much of children's blood lead comes from battery recycling, so the result is mostly uncertainty and is discounted for missing data.

rows.label: Births a year, the Philippines (2023)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: philippines, UN World Population Prospects). If unlicensed battery smelting falls, each year's newborns grow up with less lead in the air, soil and dust: the children a year of protection reaches.

rows.label: Children a year protected if the policy is adopted

rows.label: Children's average blood lead in low- and middle-income countries (µg/dL)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), from Ericson et al.'s review of blood lead in low- and middle-income countries.

rows.label: Share of Philippine children's blood lead from unlicensed battery recycling

source.title: Crawfurd L, Hu J, Mitchell T (2026), Estimating Population Lead Exposure from Battery Recycling, Center for Global Development working paper (21 January 2026)
source.quote: around 33 percent of lead exposure in low- and lower-middle-income countries may come from battery recycling
source.note: Also: LABRI, Q2 & Q3 2026 Newsletter (https://www.labrecyclinginitiative.com/post/q2-q3-2026-newsletter): 'This unlicensed recycling may be responsible for around 25% of the total lead exposure burden in the Philippines'; Ericson B et al. (2016), The global burden of lead toxicity attributable to informal used lead-acid battery sites, Annals of Global Health 82(5): 686-699 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28283119/): 127,248 to 1,612,476 DALYs in 2013.

rows.explainer: No one has measured it. The newest estimate, the Center for Global Development's 2026 paper, puts battery recycling at about a third of lead exposure in low and lower-middle income countries, with large uncertainty, and at only half a percent if just the high exposures within a few hundred metres of a site are counted. The charity's own estimate for the Philippines, from its project with the regulator, is about a quarter. An earlier site-based estimate (Ericson et al., 2016) implied under a tenth of lead's burden worldwide. The best guess weighs the two whole-population estimates: the paper's third, scaled down because the Philippines recycles a smaller share of its batteries without a licence (about 40%) than the poorest countries, and the charity's own quarter, discounted as the estimate of the organisation that proposes the fix. The near-site estimates, which leave out exposure further away, set the low end. Our judgment, 20% (3% to 35%).

rows.label: IQ points lost per µg/dL of blood lead in childhood
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), from the seven-cohort pooled analysis of Lanphear et al. (2005).

rows.label: IQ points a child keeps if unlicensed battery recycling stops
rows.explainer: Children's blood lead × unlicensed recycling's share of it × the IQ loss per µg/dL.

rows.label: Increase in earnings per IQ point
rows.explainer: The shared figure (GiveWell, {{row:iq_wage_gain}} per IQ point), read as a gain in ln(consumption).

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (GiveWell): an earner's gain is shared with the household.

rows.label: Years an IQ gain raises earnings, discounted
rows.explainer: The shared working life of 40 years (facts: givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Average years a year's smelting keeps exposing children through soil and dust
rows.explainer: Smelting puts lead in the air, which children breathe that year, and in the soil and dust around the site. Lead binds in topsoil and stays for decades unless removed or covered, which is why lead from petrol phased out decades ago still contaminates city soils; dust indoors turns over faster, and children's exposure falls as the soil near homes is covered, washed or mixed. Our judgment, an average of 10 years (3 to 30).

rows.label: Years from a child's exposure to working age
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead): lead harms the brain most before about age six, and earnings start at about 20.

rows.label: Discount for a year's smelting exposure coming over the years after
rows.explainer: The exposure a year's averted source would have caused fades at a constant rate over its life; discounted continuously at the shared rate, its present value is (1/life) ÷ (1/life + ln(1 + rate)) of the undiscounted whole.

rows.label: Discount for the waits until the earnings gain begins
rows.explainer: The exposure's spread over its life, then the years until the exposed children reach working age, at the shared rate.

rows.label: Birth cohorts' worth of exposure averted per year the smelting is stopped
rows.explainer: Each year's smelting causes that year's share of the harm for as long as its lead stays in reach: summed over that time, about one birth cohort's childhood of exposure from it. A growing number of batteries (more vehicles) puts more in each new year, and lead washed or dug away puts less. Our judgment, 1 (0.5 to 1.6).

rows.label: Earnings value per child born in the country per year of protection, in units of value
rows.formula: iq_points_per_child * iq_wage_gain * resource_sharing * iq_years * income_wait_discount * $uov_per_ln_consumption * cohorts_per_win_year
rows.explainer: IQ points kept × earnings per point × household sharing × discounted working years, after the waits, on the shared ln(consumption) scale, per cohort's worth of exposure averted.

rows.label: Deaths attributed to lead exposure worldwide, 2023
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead, from WHO and IHME's Global Burden of Disease Study 2023): lead's deaths from all sources, mostly adults' heart disease from a lifetime's exposure.

rows.label: Births worldwide, 2023
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead, UN World Population Prospects): to express lead's deaths per child born, the unit this model counts.

rows.label: People aged 65 or older, the Philippines (2023)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: philippines, UN World Population Prospects). Lead's deaths are mostly heart disease at older ages, so how many older adults the Philippines has per child born sets how many lead deaths a cut in its blood lead can avert.

rows.label: People aged 65 or older, world (2023)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead, UN World Population Prospects): the same for the world, whose lead deaths per birth the row below starts from.

rows.label: The Philippines' older adults per birth, relative to the world's
rows.explainer: The Philippines' population is younger than the world's, so a year of lower blood lead there averts fewer of the heart-disease deaths that make up most of lead's death toll. Its people aged 65 or older per birth over the world's: a proxy for the ages at which lead's deaths come (50 and over); blood lead in adults is taken as the same as the world's.

rows.label: Battery recycling's share of adults' blood lead, relative to its share of children's
rows.explainer: Adults breathe the same air and the workers who break and smelt batteries take in the most; young children, though, swallow more soil and dust by hand-to-mouth contact and absorb up to four to five times as much of what they swallow (WHO's fact sheet on lead), and adults' blood lead also comes from other work and lead stored in bone. Our judgment, 70% (30% to 120%).

rows.label: Value of a heart-disease death averted, at the world's ages (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ages of the world's cardiovascular deaths (facts: death_ages) valued by GiveWell's weights by age, the 70-and-over band split by the share at 80 or older, × the value-of-a-life slider: lead's deaths are mostly heart disease in older adults. The shared facts hold the world's age split only (and the UK's and US's); a younger country's heart-disease deaths come somewhat younger, so this slightly undervalues each death.

rows.label: Side effect: adults' lead deaths averted, value per child born per year of protection (units of value)
rows.formula: lead_deaths_2023 / world_births_2023 * age_structure_adj * source_share * adult_vs_child_exposure * lead_cvd_value_per_death * exposure_pv * cohorts_per_win_year
rows.explainer: Lead raises adults' blood pressure and heart disease. Lead's deaths per birth worldwide, scaled to the Philippines' younger population, × battery recycling's share of adults' blood lead (its share of children's × the adult ratio), valued at the shared value of a death by age, over the years the lead stays in reach. Illness short of death and kidney disease aren't counted: lead's burden is mostly deaths.

rows.label: Value per child born in the Philippines per year of protection, in units of value
rows.explainer: Children's later earnings and adults' deaths averted, per child born per year the source is kept down.

rows.label: The Philippine producer-responsibility policy's record, relative to a typical contested policy issue

source.title: LABRI, Q2 & Q3 2026 Newsletter (16 September 2026)
source.quote: Our proposals in the Philippines have recently been endorsed by a key industry stakeholder, and we are now working with government counterparts on a potential policy.

rows.explainer: For: a 2022 law already makes producers responsible for plastic packaging, so batteries can be added by extending it rather than by a new law; the regulator worked with the charity on the project; an industry body asked the environment department for such a rule in 2024 and a key industry stakeholder endorsed the charity's proposals; licensed recyclers gain from it. Against: no draft has been published, the unlicensed buyers pay more per battery than licensed ones (over 50% more in Manila), and rules on informal smelting have been weakly enforced. Our judgment, 1 (0.4 to 1.6) times the base rate.

rows.label: Chance that the Philippines adopts producer responsibility for used lead-acid batteries
rows.explainer: One event: the Philippines makes battery makers and importers responsible for collecting used batteries and having them recycled in licensed plants. The shared chance that a contested policy issue changes within about four years (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate), times the policy's own record above.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years.

rows.label: Years from the middle of the period's spending until the rule applies
rows.explainer: Counted from January 2026, the middle of the spending it is charged to. A rule extending the existing scheme needs drafting and consultation (2027 at the earliest), then time for producers to set up collection and for the regulator to act against unlicensed smelters. Our judgment, 4 years (2.5 to 7); how much of the unlicensed trade it ends is the implementation row.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the rule applies
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact of the rule
rows.explainer: The years a won reform counts, discounted, after the wait until the rule applies.

rows.label: Expected value of the Philippine policy (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Children a year × value per child × the chance of adoption × the discounted years.

Evidence adjustment: how far the lead-to-IQ-to-earnings and lead-to-heart-disease links should be trusted here
rows.explainer: The IQ loss per µg/dL comes from cohort studies that adjust for confounders but can't remove all of them (the slope is backed by the IQ gains after leaded petrol was phased out); the cohorts are from rich countries, Mexico and Yugoslavia. The IQ-to-earnings link is GiveWell's shared figure. Adults' deaths rest on the Global Burden of Disease study's blood lead to blood pressure to heart disease link, which the same caution fits. Battery recycling's share of blood lead has its own row. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), for both.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the years a won reform counts already take in that the rule would have come some day anyway, as the industry body's 2024 request shows (templates.md Convention 5); the others pressing for it are in the credit share.

rows.label: The charity's share of the research and campaigning behind the policy
rows.explainer: The charity sized the unlicensed trade, wrote the proposal and is designing the policy. Others pressing for it: the industry body that asked for a rule in 2024 and the licensed recyclers and battery makers who would gain, the policy partners the charity names, and multilateral lenders working on the problem. The environment department that adopts and enforces the rule and the producers who pay for collection are the adopters: their part is under the mobiliser's share, not this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). Unpaid research volunteers did four background reviews for the charity in early 2026 (Q1 2026 newsletter), a few percent of the resources at local wages. Our judgment, a third (15% to 60%).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Share of unlicensed smelting the rule stops in the years counted

source.title: Lead Battery Notes, How Brazil solved its lead-acid battery problem
source.quote: we do know how many ULABs are being formally recycled now — more than 75% of all batteries sold
source.note: Brazil's industry body reports over 75% of batteries sold formally recycled in 2022, after tax and producer-responsibility rules from 2005 to 2019; the share before is unsourced and no study measures the rules' effect.

rows.explainer: A rule on paper ends unlicensed smelting only as far as producers collect the batteries and the regulator acts against those who pay more for them. Brazil, after about fifteen years of tax and producer-responsibility rules, reports over three quarters of batteries sold now recycled formally, by its industry's own count and with no measure of the rules' part. In the Philippines the unlicensed buyers' price edge (about $3.50 a battery) would remain unless the scheme pays for collection, and the regulator's record against illegal smelters is weak. (Lead already in the soil is not counted as removed: the chain credits only smelting stopped.) No impact analysis gives the producers' costs, so none is counted. Sellers of used batteries would lose the unlicensed buyers' premium of about $3.50 a battery, largely money the unlicensed buyers save by skipping pollution control; at most a few percent of the modelled benefit, spread over many households, not counted. Our judgment, 40% (15% to 65%).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no policy has been adopted yet and no child's blood lead is measured; battery recycling's share of blood lead, the chance of adoption and its effect are judgments.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Side effect: the charity's guidance used beyond the Philippines, as a share of the modelled value

source.title: LABRI, Q2 & Q3 2026 Newsletter (16 September 2026)
source.quote: We recently acted as main authors on a tool published by the Partnership for a Lead-Free Future on safe management of used lead-acid batteries.

rows.explainer: It wrote the main part of a tool for officials in low- and middle-income countries on managing used batteries (August 2026), shared its Malawi findings and options with officials there, and published a review of the rules in eleven Southeast Asian countries. None of it is counted in the chain. Our judgment, a tenth more (none to 40% more).

rows.label: Share of the work towards the Philippine policy done by October 2026
rows.explainer: The market research, the project with the regulator and the proposal are done; designing the policy with government and industry, its adoption and the support its enforcement needs are still to come and will cost more. Only the share done is charged to the period's spending, so the rest of the value goes with the next dollar. Our judgment, 40% (20% to 60%).
